prompt: With `type Celsius float64`, what do `reflect.TypeOf(Celsius(21.5))` and its `Kind()` print?
hint: One is the exact type, the other the family it belongs to.

choices.text: `main.Celsius` as the type, `float64` as its kind
choices.why: Right. The type keeps its own name; the kind is what it is underneath, which is what reflective code switches on.

choices.text: `float64` and `float64`, since a named type is only an alias
choices.why: `type Celsius float64` declares a new type, not an alias, and `TypeOf` printed `main.Celsius` in the transcript.

choices.text: `main.Celsius` and `main.Celsius`
choices.why: A kind is one of 26 fixed families such as `float64` or `struct`; no program can add one, so a kind is never a type name of yours.

choices.text: `any` and `float64`, because the argument was converted to `any`
choices.why: The conversion loses the static type of the variable, but the dynamic type travels in the interface's type word, and that is what `TypeOf` returns.

prompt: `err := errors.New("disk full")` has the static type `error`. Why does `reflect.TypeOf(err)` print `*errors.errorString`?
hint: What happened to the value before `TypeOf` ran?

choices.text: `errors.New` returns a pointer, and `TypeOf` always follows pointers
choices.why: `TypeOf` follows nothing: for `&PathCount{...}` it printed `*main.PathCount`. Following a pointer is `Elem`'s job.

choices.text: Passing it as `any` kept only the dynamic type, which is the concrete one
choices.why: Right. The parameter is `any`, the interface type `error` is gone by the time the function runs, and the type word holds the concrete type.

choices.text: `error` is a built-in, so reflect has no descriptor for it
choices.why: `reflect.TypeFor[error]()` describes `error` perfectly well. It never reached `TypeOf` here because the conversion to `any` replaced it with the dynamic type.

choices.text: `TypeOf` reports the type of the function that created the value
choices.why: Types are not tied to the function that made a value; `errorString` is the type of the value itself, declared in package `errors`.

prompt: `v := reflect.ValueOf(&PathCount{"/login", 2576})` has kind `ptr`. To ask how many fields the struct has, the code first calls `v.___()`, which follows the pointer.
hint: The method that `go doc` says panics unless the kind is `Interface` or `Pointer`.

prompt: A function receives `var err error` that is nil and passes it to `reflect.ValueOf`. What does it get back?
hint: There is nothing in either word of the interface.

choices.text: The zero `Value`, whose kind is `Invalid`
choices.why: Right. A nil interface has no type word to read, so `ValueOf` returns `Value{}`, printed as `<invalid reflect.Value>`; most methods panic on it.

choices.text: A `Value` of kind `Interface` holding a nil `error`
choices.why: The static type `error` was lost when the value became an `any`, and a nil `error` becomes a nil `any`: there is no `Interface` left to report.

choices.text: A `Value` of kind `Pointer` that is nil
choices.why: That would need a type word naming some pointer type. A nil interface carries neither a type nor data.

choices.text: Nothing: `ValueOf` panics on a nil argument
choices.why: `ValueOf(nil)` returns the zero `Value` without panicking, as the last line of `typeof` showed; the panic comes later, from a method that needs a real value.

prompt: A field is declared `Method string `json:",omitempty"`` and holds `"GET"`. Under what key does `json.Marshal` write it?
hint: The tag is present, but look at what comes before the comma.

choices.text: `""`, the empty name the tag gives
choices.why: An empty name in the tag means "no name given", and the encoder falls back to the field's own name rather than writing an empty key.

choices.text: `"method"`, lower-cased by the encoder
choices.why: `encoding/json` never changes a name's case when it encodes; `Status`, untagged, went out as `"Status"`.

choices.text: `"Method"`, the name of the field itself
choices.why: Right. The tag sets only an option; with no name before the comma, the field keeps its own, which is what the `tags` program printed.

choices.text: None: a tag with no name makes the field skipped
choices.why: Skipping is what `json:"-"` asks for. `,omitempty` only skips the field when it holds its zero value, and `"GET"` is not zero.

prompt: In another package, code holds `c := reflect.ValueOf(r).FieldByName("comment")`, where `comment` is an unexported `string` field. Which call works?
hint: The `tags` program printed one of them and panicked on another.

choices.text: `c.Interface()`, which returns the string as an `any`
choices.why: That is the call that panicked: `cannot return value obtained from unexported field or method`. Handing it out as `any` would bypass the package boundary.

choices.text: `c.SetString("open")`, as long as `r` was passed by pointer
choices.why: A pointer makes a value addressable, but a field reached through an unexported name stays read-only; `CanSet` reports false either way.

choices.text: None: reflection cannot see unexported fields at all
choices.why: It can see them: `comment` appeared in the table with its tag, and `c.String()` read `busy` out of it.

choices.text: `c.String()`
choices.why: Right. Reading through a kind-specific getter is allowed; it is leaving as an `any`, or being changed, that reflection refuses.

prompt: A config loader reads tags like `env:"PORT"`. It must treat `env:""` as "never read from the environment" and a missing tag as "use the field name". What does it need?
hint: One method of `StructTag` cannot tell these two apart.

choices.text: `Tag.Get("env")` and a check for the empty string
choices.why: `Get` returns `""` both for a missing key and for an empty one, which is exactly the pair this loader must tell apart.

choices.text: `Tag.Lookup("env")`, whose second result says whether the key is there
choices.why: Right. `Lookup` returns the value and `ok`; the `tags` program showed `present=false` for `Status`, which `Get` would have reported as an empty string.

choices.text: `strings.Contains(string(f.Tag), "env")`
choices.why: That would also match a tag such as `json:"env"`, and it ignores the tag format that `Get` and `Lookup` already parse.

choices.text: `FieldByName`, which fails when the field has no tag
choices.why: `FieldByName` finds a field by its Go name and knows nothing about tags; it succeeds whether a tag is there or not.

prompt: Why does `reflect.ValueOf(x).CanSet()` report false for an `int` variable `x`?
hint: What did `ValueOf` actually receive?

choices.text: `int` is a basic type, and only struct fields can be set
choices.why: `reflect.ValueOf(&x).Elem().SetInt(25)` set the same `int` in the transcript; the kind was never the problem.

choices.text: It received a copy of `x` inside an `any`, not the variable
choices.why: Right. Converting to `any` copied the value, and setting the copy would change nothing anybody can see, so the package refuses.

choices.text: `x` was declared with `:=`, which makes it read-only to reflection
choices.why: How a variable is declared makes no difference; `x := 10` was set through its address in the same program.

choices.text: Reflection may only set variables declared in another package
choices.why: The opposite rule applies to unexported fields, and a local `int` is neither; the only missing ingredient is the address.

prompt: `reflect.ValueOf(c).MethodByName("Describ").Call(nil)` has a typo in the method's name. Where does the program fail, and saying what?
hint: What does `MethodByName` return for a name it cannot find?

choices.text: At compile time, with `Describ` undefined
choices.why: The name is a string, and the compiler checks only that `MethodByName` gets a string. The program built and ran.

choices.text: In `MethodByName`, with a panic naming `Describ`
choices.why: `MethodByName` does not complain: it returns the zero `Value`, and the name is in no message at all.

choices.text: In `go vet`, which checks method names given to `reflect`
choices.why: `go vet ./set` ran clean on this very program; no analyser reads the strings passed to `MethodByName`.

choices.text: In `Call`, with a panic about calling a zero `Value`
choices.why: Right. `MethodByName` returned the zero `Value` silently, and `Call` panicked with `call of reflect.Value.Call on zero Value`, a line away from the typo.

prompt: In package `main`, with `x := 10`, `e := reflect.ValueOf(&x).Elem()` and `c` a `Config`, which of these lines compile and pass `go vet`? Choose every one.
hint: The compiler sees the types of the arguments, never what reflection will do with them.

choices.text: `e.SetString("ten")`
choices.why: Yes. `SetString` takes a string and gets one; the mismatch with an `int` is found at run time, as a panic.

choices.text: `x = "ten"`
choices.why: Assigning a string to an `int` variable is a compile error; this is the check reflection gives away.

choices.text: `reflect.ValueOf(c).MethodByName("Describe").Call(nil)`
choices.why: Yes. It compiles and passes `go vet`, and panics with `Call with too few input arguments` when it runs.

choices.text: `c.Describe()`, with no argument
choices.why: Calling a method with too few arguments is a compile error; through `Call` the same mistake waits for the run.

prompt: In the benchmark run, `FieldDirect` took about 15.4 ns per operation and `FieldByName` between 376.3 and 409.6 ns. Roughly how many times slower is reading a field by name?
hint: Divide one by the other; any run of the three will do.

prompt: A field read by index is about 2.5 times slower than a direct one, yet `Reflect` printed the whole table only about a sixth slower than `Table`. Why?
hint: What else happens for every row besides reading two fields?

choices.text: The compiler turned the reflective calls into direct reads
choices.why: It cannot: the field index is only known at run time, from a name the user typed. The 2.5 times is measured on exactly those calls.

choices.text: Formatting and writing the table cost the same in both and dominate
choices.why: Right. `tabwriter`, `strings.Join` and the writes are shared, so the reflective part is a small slice of each operation.

choices.text: `Table` makes more allocations, which cancels out the difference
choices.why: It is the other way round: `Table` made 50 allocations and `Reflect` 58.

choices.text: Reflection only costs anything on the first call
choices.why: `FieldIndex` paid its extra on every one of millions of iterations; nothing about reflection gets cheaper after the first call unless the code caches, as `Reflect` caches indexes.

prompt: Adding `[0]` to `columns.Reflect(os.Stdout, tally.Top(s, *n)[0], …)` passed `go vet` and the compiler, and failed only when `cols` ran. What made that possible?
hint: Look at the type of `Reflect`'s second parameter.

choices.text: `go vet` skips files under `cmd/`
choices.why: `go vet ./...` covers every package in the module, `cmd/cols` included; it simply had nothing to report.

choices.text: The parameter is `any`, so every value type-checks
choices.why: Right. The compiler can only check that the argument is an `any`, which everything is; the real requirement, a slice of structs, is checked inside `Reflect` at run time.

choices.text: Indexing with `[0]` returns an interface value
choices.why: Indexing a `[]tally.PathCount` gives a `tally.PathCount`, a concrete struct; the program's own error message named it.

choices.text: A `tally.PathCount` converts automatically into a slice of one
choices.why: Go never converts on your behalf, as the `go` course put it; `Reflect` received a struct and said so.

prompt: A report loops over a million rows and calls `reflect.ValueOf(row).FieldByName(col)` for each one. Profiling shows the call on top. What is the fix that keeps the code generic?
hint: What does `columns.Reflect` do before its loop, and `encoding/json` per type?

choices.text: Replace `FieldByName` with `FieldByNameFunc` and a case-insensitive match
choices.why: `FieldByNameFunc` also walks the fields on every call, with a function call per comparison; it is no cheaper.

choices.text: Resolve the name to a field index once, before the loop, and use `Field(i)`
choices.why: Right. The name lookup is the 25-fold part; done once, each row pays only the 2.5-fold index read, which is how `fieldNamed` and the encoder's field cache work.

choices.text: Pass `&row` instead of `row`, so reflect does not copy it
choices.why: Copying a small struct is not what the profile shows; `FieldByName` searching by string is, and it searches the same way through a pointer.

choices.text: Run the loop in several goroutines
choices.why: That spreads the waste over more cores and still does a million name searches that one lookup would replace.

hint: The property a field needs before `encoding/json` will look at it.

prompt: Tests often compare results with `reflect.DeepEqual`, although reflection is slow and unchecked. Why is that an accepted use?
hint: Think about who writes the types a test helper compares, and what a test's speed is worth.

choices.text: `DeepEqual` is checked by the compiler, unlike the rest of `reflect`
choices.why: It takes two `any` values, so the compiler checks nothing about them; comparing an `int` with a `string` compiles and returns false.

choices.text: It is a test helper that must handle any type, fields included, and a test pays the run time once
choices.why: Right. It compares values of types the helper's author never saw, unexported fields too, and a few hundred nanoseconds in a test cost nobody anything.

choices.text: `DeepEqual` uses generics internally, so it costs nothing extra
choices.why: It is written with `reflect`, as its signature `DeepEqual(x, y any) bool` suggests, and walks both values at run time.

choices.text: `go test` disables reflection's panics
choices.why: A test that misuses `reflect` panics like any program; `go test` reports the panic as a failure.

prompt: A logging helper takes `v any` and must print every integer the same way, including named ones such as `type UserID int64` and `type Port uint16`. Which test picks them out?
hint: The helper cannot list types that do not exist yet.

choices.text: A type switch with `case int, int64, uint16:`
choices.why: A type switch matches exact types, and `UserID` is not `int64`: it would fall through to the default, like `main.Celsius` is not `float64`.

choices.text: Compare `reflect.TypeOf(v).String()` with `"int64"` and `"uint16"`
choices.why: `String()` of a named type is its own name, `main.UserID`, so the comparison misses exactly the named types the helper was asked to handle.

choices.text: A switch on `reflect.ValueOf(v).Kind()`, one case per integer kind
choices.why: Right. The kind is the family underneath, `int64` for `UserID` and `uint16` for `Port`, so one case per kind covers every named type anybody declares later.

choices.text: `reflect.ValueOf(v).CanInt()` alone, which also accepts unsigned kinds
choices.why: `go doc reflect.Value.CanInt` says it reports whether `Int` can be used without panicking, which is true only for the signed kinds; `Port` would be refused.
